title: NMP-PaK: Near-Memory Processing Acceleration of Scalable De Novo Genome Assembly
problem: De novo genome assembly using De Bruijn graph (DBG) algorithms is both memory-latency-bound and memory-footprint-intensive: processing 10% of the human genome (38.3 GB input) requires 528 GB of DRAM, and the Iterative Compaction step—which dominates 48% of runtime—achieves only 2.5% of available memory bandwidth due to fine-grained, irregular access patterns across large, dynamic MacroNode data structures.
motivation: Genomic datasets are growing faster than Moore's Law, and state-of-the-art distributed assemblers (e.g., PaKman) require tens of thousands of CPU cores and hundreds of terabytes of memory, making personalized medicine and microbiome analysis prohibitively costly on single-node systems.
method: The system places small processors (Processing Elements or PEs) inside DIMM buffer chips at the channel level (a near-memory processing architecture), keeping data right at the computation site instead of shuttling it back to the main CPU. Each processor runs a three-stage pipeline on data chunks called MacroNodes: Invalidation Check (discarding outdated data), TransferNode Extraction (pulling data to transfer), and Routing and Update (directing results and updating state). Within each chip, a crossbar switch routes data between processors; across different chips, a network bridge forwards TransferNodes between DIMMs. Software optimizations enhance efficiency: batching the genome into 10% chunks reduces peak memory by 14 times, pointer deduplication removes redundant MacroNode copies, and large MacroNodes (over 1 KB) are sent to the main CPU rather than overloading the processor buffers.
key_novelty: The core idea is placing pipelined processors in DIMM buffer chips (channel-level near-memory processing) and designing them specifically for MacroNode data structures, enabling the Iterative Compaction step to process many pieces in parallel with routing between chips and CPU backup for large outliers.
contributions: Systematic analysis showing that PaKman's Iterative Compaction is memory-latency-bound (54.2% stall time) with severely underutilized bandwidth (2.5% of 204.8 GB/s), making it suitable for channel-level NMP.
Channel-level NMP architecture with 3-stage pipelined systolic PEs, intra-DIMM crossbar, and inter-DIMM network bridge tailored to MacroNode-granular Iterative Compaction.
Software stack including customized batch processing (14x memory footprint reduction), pointer-aliasing deduplication, and hybrid CPU-NMP hybrid processing for irregular large MacroNodes.
16x speedup over CPU baseline, 5.7x over GPU baseline, and 8.3x throughput improvement over PaKman on a supercomputer under identical resource constraints.

metrics.speedup: 16x over CPU baseline; 5.7x over GPU (A100); 8.3x throughput vs PaKman supercomputer under same resources
metrics.accuracy: 14x memory footprint reduction; 2.4x reduction in memory operations

baselines: Software-optimized PaKman CPU baseline (Intel Xeon Platinum 8380, 40 cores)
limitations: NMP-PaK targets a single-node system; the 8.3x throughput advantage over the supercomputer reflects resource efficiency, not raw speed—the supercomputer completes full human genome assembly 123x faster in wall time.
primary_theme: Channel-level NMP acceleration of De Bruijn graph genome assembly
